title: How Lenny Rachitsky built a paid newsletter business by following energy and optimizing for curiosity
summary: Lenny explains how he stumbled into full-time writing after leaving Airbnb by tracking what energized him, and how he runs his newsletter: topic selection, a dense-advice writing style, Substack's discovery value, and niche opportunities. He also covers his angel investing and personal finance approach.

principles.text: Follow energy: do more of what energizes you and less of what drains you, then lean into the pull.
principles.quote: my philosophy was to do more of what gave me energy, and do less of what sapped me of energy. After every call, every project, every meeting, I paid attention to whether I was more energized or less energized.

principles.text: Optimize for your own curiosity over what the audience says it wants; it produces better work and keeps you sane.
principles.quote: I optimize for my own curiosity vs. what people want because it ends up being better that way, and I stay sane

principles.text: Win on density: high-quality, easy-to-understand advice, no long intros or pontification. Cut relentlessly.
principles.quote: Get to the point, synthesize it clearly, and get out of your own way.

principles.text: Frame content as a concrete, simple, direct question from a reader to anchor each post.
principles.quote: I always frame my posts as a question, since it’s an advice column, the post always starts with a concrete, simple, direct question from a reader.

principles.text: Time invested in a piece correlates strongly with performance, though some quick pieces and guest posts also win big.
principles.quote: there’s a very strong correlation between the time I put into a post and how well it does (e.g. all the posts that took 100+ hours are in the top 10)

principles.text: Stay on a platform that drives discovery and removes admin; time spent off great content is wasted, and leaving to save fees can slow growth.
principles.quote: I find that time spent on anything that isn’t making great content is wasted time, and time spent -> quality
